Title: The Sun Never Set (Part 7 of 10): The Scramble and the Summit, 1880–1913

Summary: In a single generation Britain took control of Egypt, most of the Nile valley, huge areas of East, West and southern Africa, Upper Burma and more Pacific islands, and fought the Boer War, its largest colonial war. At the same time the Indian National Congress was founded, Australia and South Africa became self-governing dominions, and new rivals rose in Germany, the US and Japan. This post covers 1880 to 1913, when the empire was at its most confident and already worried about decline.

---

## The big picture

In 1880 most of inland Africa was still ruled by Africans. By 1914 almost all of it was under European rule, with Ethiopia and Liberia the main exceptions. This was the "Scramble for Africa". Britain took the largest share by population, including Egypt, Sudan, Nigeria, the Gold Coast, Kenya, Uganda, the Rhodesias, Nyasaland, Bechuanaland and, after 1902, the Boer republics.

Conquest was made easier by new technology: quinine against malaria, steamships, railways, telegraphs, and especially the Maxim machine gun. A line from Hilaire Belloc's 1898 poem summed up the attitude: "Whatever happens, we have got / The Maxim gun, and they have not."

The empire's peak in confidence was probably Victoria's Diamond Jubilee in 1897. Two years later the Boer War showed that a small settler population could tie down nearly half a million imperial troops.

## Main timeline (1880–1899)

| Year | What happened | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| 1880–1881 | **First Boer War**; British defeat at Majuba Hill (February 1881) | The Transvaal regains self-government |
| 1881 | Mahdist uprising begins in Sudan; Urabi movement in Egypt | |
| 1882 | **Bombardment of Alexandria (July); Tel el-Kebir (September); occupation of Egypt** | Officially temporary; British troops stay until 1956 |
| 1884–1885 | Berlin Conference sets rules for European claims in Africa | No African state was invited |
| 1884 | Bechuanaland and British Somaliland protectorates; British New Guinea | |
| 1885 | **Fall of Khartoum and death of Gordon (January)**; **North-West Rebellion** in Canada; Riel hanged (November); **Indian National Congress founded** (December) | |
| 1885–1886 | **Third Anglo-Burmese War**: Mandalay taken; King Thibaw exiled; Upper Burma annexed (1 January 1886) | Years of guerrilla resistance follow |
| 1886 | Gold discovered on the Witwatersrand; Royal Niger Company chartered | Johannesburg founded; the Transvaal becomes the richest place in Africa |
| 1887 | Golden Jubilee; first Colonial Conference | |
| 1888 | Imperial British East Africa Company chartered | |
| 1889 | British South Africa Company (Cecil Rhodes) chartered | |
| 1890 | Heligoland–Zanzibar Treaty with Germany; Pioneer Column occupies Mashonaland | |
| 1893 | **First Matabele War**; Durand Line drawn between British India and Afghanistan; Gandhi arrives in South Africa | The Durand Line is still disputed by Afghanistan |
| 1894 | Uganda protectorate | |
| 1895 | East Africa Protectorate (Kenya); Chitral siege; **Jameson Raid** (December 1895 to January 1896) | The raid is a failed coup attempt against the Transvaal backed by Rhodes |
| 1896 | **Anglo-Zanzibar War** (27 August), usually listed as the shortest war in history at around 38 to 45 minutes; Ashanti expedition; bubonic plague reaches Bombay | |
| 1896–1897 | **First Chimurenga** (Second Matabele War) | Ndebele and Shona rise against Company rule |
| 1897 | **Diamond Jubilee**; Benin Expedition (February) loots the Benin Bronzes; North-West Frontier risings | |
| 1898 | Battle of **Omdurman** (2 September); Fashoda Incident with France; lease of Weihaiwei and the New Territories of Hong Kong (99 years); **Hut Tax War** in Sierra Leone | At Omdurman about 10,000 Sudanese were killed against a few dozen British and Egyptian dead. The New Territories lease is why Hong Kong was handed back in 1997 |
| 1899 | **Second Boer War begins** (October); Anglo-Egyptian condominium in Sudan | |

## Main timeline (1900–1913)

| Year | What happened | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| 1900 | Relief of Mafeking (May); British troops join the international force against the Boxers in China; **War of the Golden Stool** in Asante | |
| 1900–1902 | Boer guerrilla phase; scorched earth and **concentration camps** | About 26,000 Boer civilians (mostly children) and at least 14,000 Black Africans die in the camps |
| 1901 | **Commonwealth of Australia** (1 January); Queen Victoria dies (22 January); White Australia policy begins | |
| 1902 | Treaty of Vereeniging ends the Boer War (May); **Anglo-Japanese Alliance** | Britain abandons "splendid isolation" |
| 1903 | Conquest of the Sokoto Caliphate and Kano in northern Nigeria; Delhi Durbar for Edward VII | |
| 1903–1904 | **Younghusband expedition to Tibet** | Machine guns kill hundreds of Tibetans at Chumik Shenko (Guru) |
| 1904 | **Entente Cordiale** with France | |
| 1905 | **Partition of Bengal**; Swadeshi (boycott British goods) movement | |
| 1906 | **Bambatha Rebellion** in Natal; **Denshawai incident** in Egypt; All-India Muslim League founded; HMS *Dreadnought* launched | |
| 1907 | New Zealand becomes a dominion; Anglo-Russian Convention divides Persia into spheres of influence | |
| 1908 | Oil found at Masjed Soleyman in Persia; Alipore bomb case | The Anglo-Persian Oil Company (later BP) is founded in 1909 |
| 1909 | Morley-Minto reforms with separate Muslim electorates | |
| 1910 | **Union of South Africa** (31 May) | Self-government for the white minority; Black Africans largely excluded from the vote |
| 1911 | Delhi Durbar for George V: Bengal partition reversed and capital moved from Calcutta to Delhi | |
| 1912 | South African Native National Congress founded (later the ANC) | |
| 1913 | Natives Land Act in South Africa; Ghadar Party founded in San Francisco | The Land Act limits Black land ownership to about 7 percent of the country |

## Resistance: wars and risings against British rule

| Years | Who | Where | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1880–1881 | Transvaal Boers | South Africa | Self-government restored |
| 1880–1881 | Basotho Gun War | Basutoland | Basotho keep their guns; Basutoland later taken under direct Crown rule, which is why Lesotho is not part of South Africa |
| 1881–1898 | Mahdist state | Sudan | Destroyed at Omdurman |
| 1882 | Ahmed Urabi | Egypt | Defeated at Tel el-Kebir; exiled to Ceylon |
| 1885 | Métis and Cree under Riel, Gabriel Dumont, Big Bear and Poundmaker | Canada | Defeated; Riel and eight Indigenous men hanged |
| 1885–1895 | Burmese resistance | Upper Burma | Long guerrilla war suppressed |
| 1891–1895 | Pahang uprising | Malaya | Suppressed |
| 1893, 1896–1897 | Ndebele and Shona (First Chimurenga) | Rhodesia | Defeated; spirit medium Nehanda executed in 1898 |
| 1897 | Pashtun tribes (Malakand, Tirah) | North-West Frontier | A young Winston Churchill reports from Malakand |
| 1897 | Kingdom of Benin | Nigeria | Benin City sacked |
| 1898 | Bai Bureh, Hut Tax War | Sierra Leone | Defeated; exiled |
| 1899–1902 | Boer republics | South Africa | Defeated; annexed |
| 1900 | Yaa Asantewaa, War of the Golden Stool | Asante | Defeated; exiled to the Seychelles. The Golden Stool itself was never captured |
| 1900–1920 | Dervish state of Mohammed Abdullah Hassan | Somaliland | Lasted 20 years; ended by RAF bombing in 1920 |
| 1903–1904 | Tibet | Tibet | Forced treaty |
| 1905–1911 | Swadeshi movement and revolutionary groups | Bengal and elsewhere | Partition reversed |
| 1906 | Bambatha kaMancinza | Natal | Up to 4,000 Zulu killed |
| 1906 | Villagers of Denshawai | Egypt | Four hanged after a clash with British officers; boosts Egyptian nationalism |

## Things that happened at the same time

- **1885.** In one year: Gordon died at Khartoum, the Indian National Congress was founded, Louis Riel was hanged, Leopold's Congo Free State was created, and Britain invaded Upper Burma.
- **1896.** Ethiopia defeated Italy at Adwa, Britain fought a war against Zanzibar lasting under an hour, and the Shona and Ndebele rose in Rhodesia, all within months.
- **1898.** Omdurman (Britain), the Spanish–American War (US), and the leases of Hong Kong's New Territories and Weihaiwei happened in the same year. The "new imperialism" was not only European.
- **1899–1902.** Britain was fighting the Boers while the US fought Filipino nationalists and an international force fought the Boxers in China. Concentration camps were used in both South Africa and the Philippines, following Spain's earlier use in Cuba.
- **1904–1906.** Japan's defeat of Russia inspired anti-colonial movements across Asia. In the following two years came the Swadeshi movement, the Muslim League's founding, the Denshawai incident and the Bambatha Rebellion.

## Sources and flags

- Thomas Pakenham, *The Scramble for Africa* (1991) and *The Boer War* (1979).
- Ronald Robinson and John Gallagher, *Africa and the Victorians* (1961).
- Elizabeth van Heyningen, *The Concentration Camps of the Anglo-Boer War* (2013).
- Dan Hicks, *The Brutish Museums* (2020), on the 1897 Benin expedition.
- Charles Allen, *Duel in the Snows* (2004), on the Tibet expedition.
- South African History Online: https://www.sahistory.org.za
- **Flag:** Boer War camp death figures are the commonly cited estimates; records for Black African camps are incomplete, so their real toll is likely higher. Omdurman casualty figures come mainly from British sources. The length of the Anglo-Zanzibar War depends on which account you use. The Natives Land Act percentage (about 7 percent, later raised to about 13 percent in 1936) is the usual figure.
